trigger: ventured_claims entry (unresolved_question_gaps empty): read on C56, with C42 and C52
incumbent_reading: The paper ventures that because its practices do not secure identification in every member the organization is exposed to departures, and it counts turnover among the possible costs of intensive identification management.

wager.statement: The paper's hedge makes leaving the end that the practices come to when they fail on a member. Read as provisional, the departures in print are not that end; they come before the practices have run. Every former distributor interviewed had [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 461] (F123). Most of them had been recruited through the same upline, whose own distributorship folded that year (F123), and they left as it went. Their accounts are of an early appeal that faded (F90), of something tried that did not suit (F92), of a regular job that became satisfying (F91), of buying in to get out of an embarrassing situation at a presentation (F98). The printed figures agree that staying active is not the usual course: a secondary source puts yearly leaving between about two-fifths and nearly all of the membership (F124), and Amway's own publication counts fewer than half of recorded distributors as active (F24). The practices, meanwhile, are printed as working by repetition and over time: an achieved dream is to be replaced by a larger one (F43), no achievement is to be taken as a final peak (F44), successful distributors' aspirations shifted over time (F45), and by the author's account encapsulation grew as members spent more time with other distributors (F72). On this reading the order in C56 turns over. The leavers did not go because identification failed to take; they went early, before the repeated work the paper describes had been done on them, and identification was not secured because they had gone. Leaving in the first year is then one thing and the failure of the practices another, and the leavers in print speak only to the first. Where the practices fail would show in people who left after long, active membership. The record comes near such people twice and prints no account from either: distributors who reached high sales levels before quitting (F22), whose length of membership is not given, and distributors who moved away from positive identification (F110), of whom it is not said whether any left.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: An account from a member who left after long, active membership; or, for the leavers who are in print, a record of what each had been through in dream building and mentoring before leaving.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Absent. F123 says every former distributor interviewed left within a year. F22 and F110 report quitting after high sales and movement away from positive identification, without accounts or lengths of membership. None of F90 to F98 says what sessions, functions or mentor contact the speaker had; F97 mentions meetings and F94 a successful member's home. F125, the author's account, says the detached sought little upline advice and formed no strong bonds, which is the nearest thing to such a record and is offered as a result, not a count. The paper's own declared limit (DG03) is that it does not analyze movements between states.

strains_against: F97 -- his upline had already answered him with more meetings: the practices were being applied to him before he left.
F95 -- a leaver who frames his own dream in a persistence logic like the one he met in Amway: something of the practice had taken hold inside the year.

F94 -- he was drawn in by a successful member's home, and the paper prints displays of high-status distributors' wealth among the ways model dreams reached members (F35); the practice had arguably reached him.
F93 -- he was in long enough to see how members deferred to upline figures and to reject it.
F96 -- upline relationships that had turned irritated or openly angry are relationships that had time to form.

F89 -- the author's account is that some of those without enduring identification had felt dissatisfaction and then stopped feeling it, which has the practice working and lapsing, not arriving too late.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Former distributors of several years' active standing, or records of what each leaver attended and with whom before leaving.

fragment_jobs.F123: fixes every interviewed leaver inside the first year, which is the fact the reading turns on.
fragment_jobs.F124: gives a secondary source's range for yearly leaving, which makes leaving a common course and not an exception.
fragment_jobs.F24: gives Amway's own count that fewer than half of recorded distributors were active, so that idling without leaving is common too.
fragment_jobs.F90: prints a leaver whose account is of an early appeal that faded.
fragment_jobs.F91: prints a leaver whose regular job became satisfying and left little desire for meetings or sales work.
fragment_jobs.F92: prints a leaver who tried it and found it did not suit him.
fragment_jobs.F98: prints a leaver who bought in only to get out of an embarrassing situation, so that his joining was itself not a taking up of the dream.
fragment_jobs.F43: prints the instruction to replace an achieved dream with a larger one, one place where the practice is shown as repeated.
fragment_jobs.F44: prints the urging that no achievement be treated as a final peak, the practice again shown as without an end point.
fragment_jobs.F45: prints successful distributors' aspirations shifting over time, the practice shown as long-running.
fragment_jobs.F72: is the author's account that encapsulation grew with time spent among distributors.
fragment_jobs.F22: reports quitters who had reached high sales levels and prints nothing they said.
fragment_jobs.F110: reports movement away from positive identification over time and prints no case.

grounded_in.question: How far had each former distributor in print gone into dream building and mentoring when they stopped?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If they had been through repeated sessions and a working mentor relationship, C56 would read as written: the practices were applied, did not hold them, and the organization is exposed for that reason.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If they had seen a presentation and some meetings and no more, C56 would read as a statement about the first year of membership, where leaving comes before any test of the practices, and C27 and C28 would describe early leavers, not failed applications.

grounded_in.question: What did the distributors who quit after reaching high sales levels (F22) say of their leaving, and had they been positively identified?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If they had been positively identified and then left, C42 would have a printed case of departure from inside the practices, and turnover would read as a cost of their intensity.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If none of them had been, every departure in print would lie outside the reach of the practices, and the turnover in C42 would read as leaving that the practices had no hand in.

grounded_in.how: F123 makes the interviewed leavers people of under a year's membership; F22 reports quitters who had reached high sales levels. They point different ways on whether leaving comes before or after a member is fully engaged, and the corpus does not say whether the second group is inside the first.

rival: The first months are where the practices do their work; the paper itself holds that an organization's culture is mostly learned in the first six months (C53). Leavers of under a year are then exactly the people on whom a failure would show, and the stubs agree: the upline in F97 had tried meetings, and the leaver in F95 took the persistence logic away with him. The practices were applied and did not hold, C56 stands as written, and nothing needs turning over.

verdicts.note: KILL. The statement imports: 'Most of them had been recruited through the same upline, whose own distributorship folded that year (F123), and they left as it went.' F123 reports only that every interviewed former distributor ended membership less than a year after joining. Neither its stub nor its notes identify a shared recruiter, report that recruiter's distributorship collapsing, or connect the interviewees' departures to that collapse. No other fragment carries those assertions. The shared recruitment history, collapse, and linked departures are additions to the supplied printed record, not paraphrases or author-account drift. Separately, 'they went early, before the repeated work the paper describes had been done on them, and identification was not secured because they had gone' adds an unprinted exposure history and causal ordering. F123 supplies tenure; F43 and F44 supply exhortations to continue aspiring; F45 supplies changes in successful distributors' aspirations; F72 supplies the author's account of growing encapsulation. None establishes how much repeated work these particular leavers experienced, a minimum tenure needed for the practices to operate, or departure as the cause of unsecured identification. The card itself identifies the individual exposure histories as missing. A provisional reversal of C56 is permissible as an argument, but these asserted facts supplying it have no carrying fragment. No author-account-to-event drift was identified in the checked clauses; F72 is explicitly attributed to the author.

considered_not_fired.item: F123: first-year departures in the statement and fragment_jobs
considered_not_fired.why: F123 directly carries the claim that every former distributor interviewed left within a year. That tenure statement is cleared independently of the unsupported shared-upline narrative and exposure inference attached to it.

considered_not_fired.item: F90, F91, F92: the leavers' accounts in the statement and fragment_jobs
considered_not_fired.why: The respective stubs carry fading early appeal, a regular job becoming satisfying with little desire for meetings or sales, and trying an activity that did not suit the speaker. These are ordinary paraphrases of reported accounts.

considered_not_fired.item: F98: buying in to escape embarrassment; joining was not itself taking up the dream
considered_not_fired.why: F98 explicitly reports buying in simply to escape an embarrassing presentation under social and transportation pressure. Describing that joining motive as distinct from adopting a dream is supported. It does not establish what happened during the rest of the membership.

considered_not_fired.item: F124 and F24: turnover, inactivity, and their fragment jobs
considered_not_fired.why: F124 carries the broad annual departure estimate and its secondary-source status; F24 carries fewer than half of recorded distributors being active. Describing departures and inactivity as common summarizes those figures. These figures do not establish individual exposure histories or the cause of departure.

considered_not_fired.item: F43, F44, F45, F72: repetition and change over time
considered_not_fired.why: F43 carries replacing an achieved dream with a larger one; F44 carries continued striving without a final peak; F45 carries aspirations shifting over time. F72 is accurately identified as the author's account of encapsulation increasing with time among distributors. These descriptions and fragment jobs are supported; their extension into a first-year exposure threshold is not.

considered_not_fired.item: F22 and F110: high-sales quitters and changes in identification
considered_not_fired.why: F22 reports high sales before quitting without supplying those quitters' testimony or tenure. F110 reports identification changes without supplying an individual departure account or identifying which people left. The card preserves these uncertainties. The absence of detailed transitions is also consistent with DG03.

considered_not_fired.item: C56, C42, C52 and the proposed long-membership comparison
considered_not_fired.why: The opening characterization has a basis in the claims' stated links between unsuccessful identification management, departure, and possible organizational costs. Disputing those links is not itself an import. Requesting testimony from long-active leavers is a proposed evidentiary test, not an assertion that such testimony is printed. The kill concerns added factual premises, not disagreement with the incumbent theory.

verdicts.note: CLEAR. All 125 fragment stubs were examined, with their notes, the declared gaps, and the absence register. No eligible fragment supplies an event the reading necessarily cannot accommodate. The closest direct evidence that practices had reached the interviewed leavers is either a seed or explicitly declared under strains_against. Other fragments show practices reaching newcomers, effects during particular encounters, or continuing relationships among inactive members, but do not establish the interviewed leavers' exposure histories or a contrary departure sequence. The absence of those histories supports the B finding of an unsupported assertion; it is not affirmative contradictory evidence for E. Disagreement with claims or with a stub explicitly reporting only the author's account was not treated as contradiction of an event.

considered_not_fired.why: The card explicitly declares all six as strains. They include rejection of upline authority, attraction to a model dream, persistence language, troubled upline ties, and reliance on more meetings. Even where these challenge the assertion that practices had not run, declared strains cannot fire E. F89 additionally reports the author's explanation.

These are seeds and therefore excluded from E kills. F22 supplies high-sales quitters without tenure or exposure histories; F110 supplies identification transitions without establishing departure. Neither supplies the missing long-active leaver account.

These describe training newer members, dream-building encounters, and instruction to copy mentors; F37 even places dream building before prospects. They challenge any universal assertion that practices begin only after a year. The card's specific missing fact, however, concerns how much repeated work the interviewed leavers experienced. These fragments do not identify their exposure or departure sequence, so they do not independently contradict that proposed sequence. F28 explicitly reports the author's account.

considered_not_fired.item: F112 through F119, especially F115 and F116
considered_not_fired.why: The shopping outing shows instruction and a change in the researcher's behavior within the outing. It does not show that an interviewed leaver received sustained practices, secured identification, and subsequently left. Immediate effects in another participant can coexist with the proposed distinction between initial contact and repeated work.

F74 reports difficult opening months because of outsiders' reactions. F80 reports a participant's view that remaining active generally requires close upline support. Neither reports the disputed leavers' exposure or rules out early departure interrupting further practice.

These concern permeable membership boundaries, inactive members' continuing aspirations and support, mixed reactions, or the researcher's role strain. Inactivity and continuing ties do not entail departure after long active membership. F70 and F107 are explicitly author accounts. The card can accommodate these distinctions without changing their reported events.

The fragments explicitly report the author's explanatory account of practices and identification. F99's failed-sensegiving sequence and F125's explanation of weak bonds are particularly close to the contested causal order, but do not independently report the leavers' exposure histories. The listed claims are theory, including C53's assertion about learning in the first six months. Disagreeing with these accounts or claims cannot fire E.

The ex-member website urges departure without supplying an individual history of long active membership and practice failure. DG03 explicitly limits analysis of identification transitions. A01 concerns unavailable comparable profit figures, A02 unprinted refused-recruit testimony, and A03 an unavailable official turnover rate. None supplies the missing exposure or departure history, and missing evidence is not a contradiction.

attack.kept: A killed reading is retained, marked. Deleting it removes the evidence that the pass functions.
